title: The poem and its text
short: A definition poem from about 1861-62 (Franklin 314), printed in 1891; Dickinson's manuscript puts 'Hope' in quotation marks.
body: The poem survives in Fascicle 13, one of the hand-sewn booklets Dickinson made around 1861; Johnson dates it 1861, and Franklin's later editions put it about 1862. Franklin numbers it 314 (Johnson 254). It was first printed in Poems: Second Series (1891), edited by Higginson and Todd, whose text the archive follows. That edition regularised Dickinson's punctuation: the manuscript puts "Hope" in quotation marks, as if the word itself were being defined, and uses dashes throughout ('And sweetest - in the Gale - is heard -'). Students quoting the poem should know which text they use; Franklin's and Miller's editions give the manuscript form.

title: the thing with feathers
short: Hope is defined as a bird by riddling understatement: "the thing with feathers" names the creature by a single attribute.
body: Dickinson often writes definition poems ('Hope is ...', 'Faith is a fine invention'), and here she defines an abstraction with a riddle: not 'a bird' but 'the thing with feathers'. The vagueness of 'thing' keeps the metaphor strange and slightly comic. Feathered hope has biblical associations: God shelters the faithful under his 'feathers' (Psalm 91:4). The bird that 'perches in the soul' turns the soul into a tree or perch, a domestic, homely image of an inner state.

title: Hope as a winged figure
short: Hope has an ancient iconography, from Hesiod's Pandora myth onward; Dickinson domesticates it as a small songbird.
body: In Hesiod's Works and Days, when Pandora opens the jar of evils, Hope (Elpis) alone remains inside; and allegorical tradition often depicted Hope with wings, an anchor or a bird. Dickinson takes the familiar personification and makes it modest: not a goddess but a 'little bird'. Hesiod's story is itself ambiguous (is Hope a blessing kept for men, or one more evil?), and Dickinson elsewhere offers a darker view: in 'Hope is a subtle Glutton' (Franklin 1493) hope feeds on what it desires. The two poems are often read together.

anchor: sings the tune without the words
title: the tune without the words
short: Hope is a wordless song: it cannot state reasons or promises, yet it never stops.
body: Hope's song has melody but no words: it carries feeling without propositional content, as hope persists without evidence. Some readers hear an echo of the vogue for Mendelssohn's piano 'Songs without Words' (Lieder ohne Worte) in nineteenth-century parlours, though there is no evidence Dickinson intended it. 'And never stops at all' is deliberately plain; the colloquial 'at all' gives the line the tone of a child's assertion, typical of Dickinson's mixing of hymn and speech.

anchor: sweetest in the gale is heard
title: sweetest in the gale
short: Hope sounds sweetest in adversity, when the storm is strongest; a paradox central to the poem.
body: A gale is a strong wind. The paradox is that the bird's song is 'sweetest' when conditions are worst, as hope matters most in trouble. Dickinson's manuscript isolates the words with dashes ('And sweetest - in the Gale - is heard -'), slowing the line so that each phrase is felt; the 1891 text runs it together. The word order (verb last, 'is heard') is a hymn-like inversion.

title: sore
short: 'Sore' here means severe, grievous: only a terrible storm could silence the bird.
body: 'Sore' as an adjective or adverb of intensity ('sore afraid', 'a sore famine') is common in the King James Bible and was old-fashioned even in Dickinson's day. Webster defines it in this sense as violent or severe. The line implies that no ordinary storm could defeat hope; it would take an exceptional one, and the poem never says that such a storm has come.

anchor: That could abash the little bird
title: abash
short: To 'abash' is to disconcert or put to shame; the storm would have to silence the bird by embarrassing it, a wittily human verb.
body: 'Abash' (Old French esbahir, to astonish) means to destroy someone's self-possession, to confound or make ashamed. Applied to a bird in a storm it is unexpected: the storm is imagined not as killing the bird but as discountenancing it, making it lose its nerve. The personification keeps the poem's tone light. 'That kept so many warm' gives the bird a further role: hope, though small, warms many people, perhaps like a bird brooding over its young.

title: the chillest land ... the strangest sea
short: Extremes of cold and strangeness, emotional or literal, where the speaker has heard hope sing.
body: The superlatives 'chillest' and 'strangest' (Dickinson freely forms such superlatives) suggest the farthest regions of experience, perhaps of despair, isolation or the unknown. Dickinson rarely travelled, so the land and sea are generally read as inner states, in keeping with the soul as the bird's perch. 'I 've heard it' (the 1891 spacing) shifts from definition to personal testimony, as in a church testimony of faith.

title: extremity
short: 'Extremity' is the utmost point of need or danger; even then, hope asked for nothing.
body: Webster gives 'extremity' as the utmost point, and also the utmost distress or necessity. The line praises hope's generosity: it gives warmth and song and never takes. Dickinson's manuscript reads 'Yet - never - in Extremity, / It asked a crumb - of me.', capitalising the key words and ending on the self. Some critics hear a note of irony: hope asks nothing, but does it give anything real? The poem leaves that question open.

anchor: It asked a crumb of me
title: a crumb
short: Hope needs no feeding; the crumb recalls both feeding birds in winter and the Gospel's crumbs from the master's table.
body: Feeding birds with crumbs in winter is the literal picture. A biblical undertone may be heard in Matthew 15:27, where the Canaanite woman says 'yet the dogs eat of the crumbs which fall from their masters' table', a story of persistent, humble faith rewarded. Here the roles are reversed: hope sustains the speaker and asks nothing in return. The final line closes the poem with understatement, the bird's selflessness becoming the measure of its value.

title: Hymn metre
short: Three quatrains in loose common metre (the hymn or ballad stanza), alternating four- and three-stress lines, with full and slant rhymes.
body: Dickinson's favourite form is the hymn stanza she knew from Isaac Watts and the Protestant hymnal: lines of four and three iambic stresses alternating (the first line is a seven-syllable variation on the pattern). Stanza 1 rhymes only on lines 2 and 4, and slantly ('soul/all'); stanza 2 rhymes alternately ('heard/bird', 'storm/warm'); stanza 3 rhymes 'sea/me' fully, with 'extremity' echoing them in line 3. The hymn form lends a devotional frame to a poem that never mentions God, a characteristic Dickinson strategy of using the church's music for private meanings.
